A1-A2.headline: The History of the Medieval Balkan Slave Trade

pages.text:
Why were thousands of people moved across the old Adriatic Sea? From the 600s to the mid-1400s, the Balkan slave trade ran as a big network.

Ships from Venice took people to Southern Europe and the Middle East.
pages.caption: Slavic populations living in the medieval Balkan region.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Први Словени између Дунава и Балкана.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Illustration of Sclaveni between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains

pages.text:
This sad trade grew because the Balkans sat between different faiths. Old local rules did not let groups sell people of the same faith.

People of other beliefs were seen as fair targets. Because of that rule, pagan, Orthodox Christian, and Bogomil groups became main sources for sellers.

People in Bosnia who followed the Bogomil faith were hit hardest. Main churches did not accept their group, so they had little outside help when sea sellers came.

Big profits from this wide trade helped build the Republic of Venice into a rich, strong sea state across the area.

Many women were sold as home workers in Italy and Spain. Each year, ships also carried thousands of young boys to the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt.

There, the boys trained as top army fighters called Mamluks. They kept army power strong until Ottoman rule changed the area.

B1-B2.headline: Venice and the Medieval Balkan Slave Trade Network

pages.text:
What drove the movement of thousands across the medieval Adriatic Sea? From the 7th to the mid-15th century, the Balkan slave trade formed a major network.

Venetian traders shipped captives to Southern Europe and the Middle East.
pages.caption: Illustration depicting Slavic groups in the Balkan region.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Први Словени између Дунава и Балкана.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Illustration of Sclaveni between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains

pages.text:
This trade expanded because the Balkans sat along a religious border zone. Medieval custom strictly barred the sale of fellow believers. People of other faiths, however, were treated as lawful targets.

As a result, pagan, Orthodox Christian, and Bogomil groups became key sources for coastal merchants.

Bosnians who practiced Bogomilism faced heavy targeting because mainstream churches rejected their faith. With few strong allies nearby, local towns were left exposed to capture.

Profits from this wide trade helped build the Republic of Venice into a rich sea-trading empire.

While women were often sold into home work in Italy and Spain, thousands of young boys sailed yearly to the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt.

These youths trained as elite soldier-slaves known as Mamluks. They backed army power across the region until Ottoman conquest reshaped the map.

C1-C2.headline: Geopolitics and Religious Frontiers in the Balkan Slave Trade

pages.text:
What propelled the forced displacement of thousands across the medieval Adriatic? Spanning the 7th to mid-15th centuries, the Balkan slave trade thrived.

Venetian merchants dispatched captives across Southern Europe and the Middle East.
pages.caption: Depiction of Sclaveni populations.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Први Словени између Дунава и Балкана.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Illustration of Sclaveni between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains

pages.text:
This commercial network flourished precisely because the Balkans constituted a contested confessional frontier. Medieval custom strictly proscribed enslaving coreligionists, yet heterodox populations remained deemed permissible targets.

Consequently, pagan, Orthodox Christian, and Bogomil communities became principal reservoirs for maritime traffickers.

Bosnian adherents of Bogomilism suffered disproportionate targeting because ecclesiastical authorities withheld recognition from their doctrine as orthodox Christianity.

Substantial revenues accrued from this pervasive trafficking proved instrumental in consolidating the Republic of Venice as a preeminent Mediterranean maritime empire.

Whereas women were predominantly marketed as domestic laborers throughout Italy and Spain, thousands of boys were transported annually to Egypt's Mamluk Sultanate.

Trained as elite military retainers termed Mamluks, these cohorts sustained dynastic hegemony until Ottoman expansion fundamentally transformed regional geopolitics.
